title: Analysis of James Webb data reveals the power of galactic winds
excerpt: Galactic winds from the centers of massive galaxies may have suppressed star formation. But data from the James Webb Space Telescope revealed an unexpected aspect of these outflows.
content:
Powerful gas outflows from the centers of massive galaxies probably suppressed star formation during the era when it was at its most intense. Observations by the James Webb Space Telescope have shown that such outflows occur more frequently and are more powerful than astronomers previously thought. However, in most cases, they only slow down this process. Outflows driven by supermassive black holes are most likely responsible for stopping it completely.

Gas leaves galaxies

Between 12 and 8 billion years ago, stars in the Universe formed more actively than at any other time, before or since. Astronomers call this period cosmic noon.

Rebecca Davies of Swinburne University of Technology in Melbourne and Sirio Belli of the University of Bologna have summarized observations of massive galaxies from cosmic noon made by the James Webb Space Telescope in a review article. The telescope has made it possible to measure how much of the cold gas from which stars form is carried out of these galaxies by outflows. It turned out that such flows are more common and more powerful than previously thought, meaning that galaxy evolution depends heavily on them. The review will be published in the journal Astrophysics and Space Science, and its text is currently available on arXiv.

How James Webb is changing our understanding of star formation. Credit: James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) YouTube channel.

Stars form from cold gas, which contracts under its own gravity into dense clouds. If the gas runs out or becomes too hot or turbulent, these clouds do not form. Therefore, how long star formation continues in a galaxy determines whether new planetary systems, including potentially habitable ones, can emerge there.

Equilibrium instead of quenching

Outflows are generated by supernova explosions or by energy released when matter falls into a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy. As Rebecca Davies explains in comments cited by Phys.org, growing black holes produce powerful winds that blow away gas suitable for star formation. The energy released by a black hole can either expel gas from a galaxy or heat it so much that it can no longer contract. According to James Webb observations, outflows of this origin are associated with the rapid quenching of star formation.

However, outflows are very common in massive galaxies during cosmic noon, yet most of these galaxies do not quench their star formation at all. According to Rebecca Davies, outflows mostly remove only part of the gas, so a galaxy does not use up its entire supply to form stars too quickly and can continue producing them. What triggers the most powerful outflows remains unknown. Among the possible causes, the astrophysicist mentions galaxy mergers and radio jets — narrow streams of matter ejected from the vicinity of a central black hole.

A chance for the Solar System

As massive galaxies age, the activity of their central black holes weakens. The same happened to the Milky Way, whose black hole, Sagittarius A*, is now relatively inactive, although, according to Rebecca Davies, a powerful outburst occurred near it several million years ago. Weaker ejections took place only a century or two ago, while the brightness near the black hole fluctuates almost daily because of hot gas orbiting nearby.

If our Galaxy had quenched its star formation back during cosmic noon, few new stars would probably have formed in it over the past 10 billion years, explains Sirio Belli. The Solar System, which is only 5 billion years old, would never have formed either. For astrobiologists, this means that a planet’s habitability should be assessed together with the star formation history of its host galaxy, rather than considering only its parent star.

Excessively intense star formation also has a downside, because frequent supernova explosions can negatively affect the habitability of planets. According to Sirio Belli, astronomers are only beginning to investigate how processes on galactic scales affect conditions on individual planets.
